html:
Horse domestication is the taming and breeding of the horse, which ancient DNA now traces to the Pontic Caspian steppe, around the lower Volga and Don rivers, about 2200 BCE. All modern domestic horses descend from that one population.

People had hunted wild horses for tens of thousands of years. The older view put the first domestic horses at Botai in Kazakhstan around 3500 BCE, where horses were kept and possibly milked. Genetic studies found that the Botai horses were not the ancestors of today's horses, and their use may have been closer to managing wild herds. The herders of the Yamnaya expansion used wagons but probably did not rely on riding.

After about 2200 BCE the new horses spread fast across Eurasia, and with them came a new kind of power:

  • The Sintashta culture built the earliest spoke-wheeled chariots around 2000 BCE. Chariots soon reached Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and China.
  • Riding on horseback became common later, in the first millennium BCE. It made the mounted archers of the Scythians and the Xiongnu possible.
  • Steppe empires, up to the Mongol Empire, were built on horses.

Settled states wanted horses badly. Han China even fought the War of the Heavenly Horses to get them from Ferghana. In the Americas, horses arrived only with the Spanish, and horses on the plains changed life there after 1700.
